item.title: Studies on Avoided Affect across Latin America, South Korea, and the U.S. — Fri Oct 16, 11:00 AM — Erwin Square Building
item.description: Prior research suggests that individuals in Latin American cultures value positivity, striving for and expressing positive emotions more than East Asian individuals and at times experiencing them more than European American individuals. Paradoxically, Latines also avoid negative emotions less than European Americans. To better understand these patterns, this research examines cultural variation in affect valuation across East Asian, Latin American, and U.S. cultural contexts, asking participants which emotions they a) ideally want to feel, b) actually feel and c) want to avoid. Studies 1 and 2 compare ideal, actual, and avoided affect across samples from Ecuador, Colombia, South Korea, and the U.S., considering emotions that vary in both arousal and social engagement. Study 3 extends this work by examining associations with personal values, interpersonal goals, and well-being among Colombian, South Korean, and U.S. American individuals. item.description: Omics technologies are increasingly being used to support product safety assessment in agricultural chemistry development, offering new opportunities to understand biological responses with greater depth, context, and mechanistic resolution. This seminar will explore the role of omics in product safety for agricultural chemicals, beginning with early-stage R&D applications such as compound characterization, mode-of-action exploration, biological profiling, and prioritization of candidates with more favorable safety profiles. The discussion will then move to later-stage development, focusing on the incorporation of omics into short term in vivo study designs to provide mechanistic context for traditional toxicology endpoints, evaluate biological relevance, and support integrated weight-of-evidence conclusions. item.title: On the Possibility of a Division of Moral Labor — Fri Oct 16, 3:20 PM — West Duke 202
item.description: Many descriptions of human nature imagine that human variation is variation around a central tendency or "normal" human form. This makes a lot of sense. Many human traits do seem nearly universal in humans (e.g. a bilateral bodily organization). Similarly, many descriptions of human moral psychology hypothesize that humans have a central or normal core of morality. For example, some moral philosophers view nearly every human as recognizing certain "moral fixed points" that can constrain moral theorizing. And many moral psychologists aim to characterize the moral capacities typical of humans. These philosophical and psychological views tend to view moral variation as noise around a central human form. Other ethical idealizations also tend to involve appeal to a unitary norm (e.g. the idea of the morally virtuous person). item.title: Nonparametric Inference for Nonstationary Spatial Point Processes — Fri Oct 16, 3:30 PM — None
item.description: Point pattern data often exhibit features such as abrupt changes, hotspots and spatially varying dependence in local intensity. Under a Poisson process framework, these correspond to discontinuities and nonstationarity in the underlying intensity function. These features are difficult to capture with standard modeling approaches. This seminar proposes a spatial Cox process model in which nonstationarity is induced through a random partition of the spatial domain, with conditionally independent Gaussian process priors specified across the resulting regions. This construction allows for heterogeneous spatial behavior, including sharp transitions in intensity. A discretization-free MCMC algorithm is developed to target the infinite-dimensional posterior distribution without approximation, thus ensuring exact inference. item.title: Allie Martin and Brittany Green: Sampling for Black Life — Fri Oct 16, 4:00 PM — Biddle Music Building
item.description:
This event includes a presentation by ethnomusicologist Allie Martin and a discussant's remarks from composer Brittany Green.
Sampling for Black Life: The ethics of music sampling, often limited to copyright law and intellectual property, raise concerns about how Black voices and sounds have been tried on, used, and discarded in commercial and archival work. When it comes to sampling, what is owed to the voices and soundscapes on archival recordings of Black life, which were often obtained under questionable circumstances? Drawing on materials sampled during a residency at the Library of Congress, I introduce a practice of "sampling with critical intention" that engages these materials with rigorous care. This talk offers an artistic intervention aimed toward liberatory amplification, insisting that sampling has the potential to disrupt anti-Black violence both in and out of the archive.
This event is free and open to the public. All are welcome!
Source: Duke University

item.title: NCLAFF. OUR LAND (NUESTRA TIERRA) — Fri Oct 16, 7:00 PM — None
item.description:
Nuestra Tierra. 2025. Dir. Lucrecia Martel (Argentina). 122 min. DCP
In 2009, a man and two accomplices try to evict members of the Indigenous community of Chuschagasta in northern Argentina. Claiming ownership of the land and armed with guns, they kill the community's leader, Javier Chocobar. The murder is caught on video. It takes nine years of protests before court proceedings are finally opened in 2018. During all this time, the killers remain free. The film combines the voices and photographs of the community with courtroom footage to explore the long history of colonialism and land dispossession that led to this crime. October 16. Ruby Film Theatre. 7:00 pm

In October 2009, Javier Chocobar, a member of the indigenous Chuchagasta community in northwest Argentina's Tucumán Province, tried to defend himself and his people from being forcibly evicted from their land by a local landowner and two former police officers. As a result, the 68-year-old Chocobar was shot and killed, and two other community members were wounded. The murder is caught on video. It takes nine years of protests before court proceedings are finally opened in 2018. During all this time, the killers remain free.

item.description:
Spend an afternoon learning about woody plants with ethnobiologist marc williams. This in-person intensive class begins with a presentation about major tree and shrub families. Then head outside on a plant walk to learn how to identify woody trees and shrubs by their leaves, bark, flowers, fruit and growing conditions, and learn to spot characteristic clues to determine the plant families to which they belong. Discussion will include common and obscure uses for woody plants that can support overall human health, well-being and sustenance, along with relationships between woody plants and fungi. item.title: NC the Beautiful: Invasive Plant Purge — Sat Nov 21, 12:00 PM — Haw River State Park - Iron Ore Belt Access
item.description:
“Invasive” plants are introduced, aggressively-growing plants that negatively impact local ecosystems. Join park staff at Haw River State Park’s Iron Ore Belt Access to help remove these leafy invaders!
Typical workdays start with paperwork for new volunteers (less than five minutes) followed by a short hike to the work area where volunteers will receive instruction on how to identify the target species of the day. The rest of the time will be used on employing hands-on, seasonally appropriate techniques to remove invasive plants from the landscape, helping to restore the area for native plants and wildlife.
Advance registration is required as supplies and space are limited. This opportunity is only open to volunteers ages 12 and up. Any volunteers under the age of 16 must be registered with and accompanied by an adult.
